stops.name: Frankfurt am Main, the house on the Großer Hirschgraben
stops.campa: At the stroke of noon on 28 August, as the bells of Frankfurt ring, a son is born to the imperial councillor Johann Caspar Goethe and his young wife Catharina Elisabeth. The child comes into the world blue and seemingly lifeless; only the grandmother's persistence rouses him to breath. The planets, he will later write, stood in a friendly aspect: the sun in Virgo, the moon full. In the tall patrician house on the Hirschgraben the boy will be raised among books, engravings of Rome, and the free imperial city's proud liberties.
stops.quote: On the 28th of August, 1749, at mid-day, as the clock struck twelve, I came into the world, at Frankfort-on-the-Main. My horoscope was propitious: the sun stood in the sign of the Virgin, and had culminated for the day.

stops.name: Frankfurt, the puppet-theatre in the gable room
stops.campa: At Christmas the grandmother gives the children a puppet-theatre, and the four-year-old is enchanted past all measure. Behind the little proscenium the boy learns to move wooden kings and devils, to speak their parts, to invent whole plays. The passion never leaves him; the marionettes of David and Goliath become, decades later, the raw seed of Faust and of Wilhelm Meister's theatrical mission. Here, in play, the dramatist is first born.

stops.name: Frankfurt, the news of the Lisbon earthquake
stops.campa: On All Saints' Day word comes that Lisbon, a great and splendid capital, has been swallowed in an instant by earthquake, fire and flood, sixty thousand dead at prayer in their churches. The six-year-old hears the grown people dispute the goodness of God who lets the just perish with the wicked. The daemon of terror, he will write, never spread so swiftly over the earth. The child's serene trust in the Almighty is shaken; the first crack of theodicy opens in him, and he cannot mend it.
stops.quote: God, the Creator and Preserver of heaven and earth, whom the explanation of the first article of the creed represented as so wise and benignant, had, in permitting the just and the unjust to perish together, by no means acted in a fatherly manner.

stops.name: Frankfurt, the French occupation and Count Thoranc
stops.campa: In the Seven Years' War the French seize Frankfurt, and the king's lieutenant, the art-loving Count Thoranc, is quartered in the Goethe house. The father, loyal to the Emperor and Prussia, grows bitter under the foreign guest; the boy delights instead in the painters Thoranc commissions, watching pictures made before his eyes and learning to love the theatre the French bring to town. He picks up their tongue in the streets. Discord at the hearth teaches him early the ambiguity of great events.

stops.name: Frankfurt, the coronation of Joseph II and the Gretchen affair
stops.campa: The imperial city fills for the coronation of Joseph II as King of the Romans; the fourteen-year-old wanders the festal crowds in secret company of an older girl, Gretchen, of a lower station, whom he loves with a boy's whole heart. He holds her hand, is once kissed upon the brow. But her circle is entangled in a forgery scandal, and when it breaks she says she felt for him only as a sister. The humiliation is his first grief in love; the name Gretchen he will carry to the scaffold of Faust.

stops.name: Frankfurt, the sister Cornelia and the Bible in verse
stops.campa: Closest of all to him is his sister Cornelia, a year younger, dark, ardent and unhappy, his confidante and first reader. Together they are drilled by the father in the strict domestic school, learning languages, drawing, music, riding and fencing. The precocious boy writes verse in many tongues, sets Joseph's story from the Bible into rhyme, and burns some of it in a fit of self-judgment. In the tall house, under the paternal rule, the future poet is already ceaselessly making. Cornelia's later grief will haunt him.

stops.name: Leipzig, matriculation at the university
stops.campa: The father sends the boy of sixteen to Leipzig to study law. He arrives in the elegant merchant city they call Little Paris, and law bores him to distraction; he attends instead the lectures of Gellert on style, learns drawing under Oeser, and remakes himself into a dandy of the newest French cut. He falls in love with Käthchen Schönkopf, the innkeeper's daughter, and pours his jealous heart into the light rococo verses of Annette and into his first plays. The provincial burgher becomes a poet of the salon.

stops.name: Leipzig: Auerbachs Keller and Oeser's drawing school
stops.campa: In the vaulted wine-cellar of Auerbach's, its walls painted with the legend of Doctor Faustus riding out on a barrel, the student drinks and observes. Under Adam Friedrich Oeser at the drawing academy he learns to see line and proportion, and through Oeser first hears the name of Winckelmann and the noble simplicity of the Greeks. Art, not law, is schooling him. The Faust of the cellar-wall lodges in his imagination and waits.

stops.name: Leipzig, the hemorrhage, the near-death
stops.campa: In the night the young man wakes in terror; his lungs hemorrhage and he loses a great quantity of blood, and for days lies at the edge of death. A tumor swells at his neck. The gay Leipzig life is over. Broken in body, having taken no degree, he is carried home to Frankfurt to convalesce or to die. In sickness he turns inward, and the vanity of the dandy falls away.

stops.name: Frankfurt, convalescence with Susanna von Klettenberg, the alchemy
stops.campa: Through the long recovery he is nursed in spirit by Susanna Katharina von Klettenberg, a Pietist mystic and Moravian, kinswoman of his mother, a soul so serene he will draw her whole as the Beautiful Soul of Wilhelm Meister. With her and the physician Metz he reads the alchemists: Paracelsus, Welling, the Aurea Catena Homeri. He sets up a small furnace in the attic to seek the liquor of the philosophers, the Virgin Earth, the salt of salts. The hermetic dream of one living force behind all matter enters him and never wholly leaves.

stops.name: Strasbourg, arrival and the Münster
stops.campa: He comes to Strasbourg to finish his law, and on the very first day climbs the red sandstone tower of the cathedral. The soaring Gothic minster, which the French taste of his schooling had taught him to despise as barbarous, strikes him instead as a living organic whole, grown like a tree of God: the work of the master Erwin von Steinbach. He climbs the platform daily to cure his dread of heights, and writes in praise of German architecture, calling the Gothic no longer barbarous but sublime.
stops.quote: How refreshing it was to me to view this in the presence of the work itself and to pronounce it good, as God did after each of his days of creation.

stops.name: Strasbourg: Herder and the opening of the eyes
stops.campa: In an inn on the way lies Johann Gottfried Herder, come to be couched for a fistula of the eye, ill-tempered and magnificent. The younger man attends him through the painful cure and drinks in his teaching: distrust the French rules, learn to read Shakespeare as a force of nature, gather the folk-songs of the people as the true voice of poetry, feel Homer and Ossian and the Bible as living speech. Herder turns his gaze from wit to nature, from the salon to the nation. The Sturm und Drang is kindled here.
